title: Relationship between slag layer and in-situ nanoparticle formation in PBF–LB using reactive atmospheres
abstract: Abstract Oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) materials are typically processed using powder metallurgy routes or additive manufacturing to ensure homogeneous nanoparticle distribution in the materials. Processing routes where the nanoparticles are formed during manufacturing (in-situ) can effectively prevent problems occurring in ex-situ routes (e.g. powder blending) such as nanoparticle agglomeration. One of the approaches to manufacture in-situ ODS materials is the use of reactive process gases during powder bed fusion–laser beam (PBF–LB). Processing with carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) causes O uptake, which promotes nanoparticle formation. Manufacturing in CO 2  is accompanied by the formation of surface slag layers on the samples, whose effect on nanoparticle formation is yet unclear. In this work, the role of the slag layer on the formation of nanoparticles, as well as the layer formation mechanism, is studied. For this purpose, a model alloy, consisting of pure Fe alloyed with 4.3 wt% Ti is processed in CO 2,  and the influence of the powder layer height, sample height, and re-melting on slag layer and nanoparticle formation is investigated. Results show that nanoparticles do not originate from the slag layer. Instead, the slag layer is formed by liquid nanoparticles floating to the surface of the melt pool. The slag layer accumulates from layer to layer until the slag layer thickness converges to a steady value. This work contributes to the understanding of particle formation mechanisms occurring in melt pools in additive manufacturing processes, which is necessary to define the requirements for alloy design of advanced in-situ particle reinforced ODS materials.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) materials offer excellent high temperature properties, e.g. high temperature strength and creep resistance, which makes them ideal candidates for applications in turbine engines and aerospace engineering [ 1 ]. Fe-based ODS materials stand out from this broad group of materials as they additionally offer high radiation tolerance for applications in nuclear power reactors and similar environments [ 2 ]. Additive manufacturing (AM) is nowadays frequently used to manufacture components from these materials, as processing nanoparticle-containing powder blends is difficult by conventional manufacturing routes, e.g. casting. There are ex-situ and in-situ approaches when introducing nanoparticles. Ex-situ approaches include ball milling and powder blending [ 3 ,  4 – 5 ]. In-situ approaches are routes where the nanoparticles form during AM processes. Oxygen (O) is either introduced during gas atomization [ 6 ,  7 ], by oxide particles with low stability [ 8 ,  9 ] or during manufacturing with O-containing process atmospheres [ 10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ]. Nanoparticles form in the materials by reactions between O and the alloying elements in the melt pool. High levels of O in the materials are desired to increase particle formation.

Instead of using small O additions in an argon (Ar) atmosphere in the process chamber, more reactive atmospheres such as pure nitrogen (N 2 ) or carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) are potential candidates for in-situ nitride and oxide formation in AM processes [ 15 ,  16 ,  17 ,  18 – 19 ]. The interaction between material and process gas using an N 2  atmosphere for Fe-based materials is low compared with CO 2  and often requires alloying to increase the reaction with N 2  [ 20 ], hence, CO 2  might be a better choice to process in-situ particle reinforced materials in PBF–LB.

Regardless of the chosen approach to manufacturing ODS materials in AM, most authors concentrate on the properties of the bulk microstructure and neglect the formation of slag and slag layers at the sample surface. The formation of oxide-rich slag layers is especially relevant when manufacturing in reactive atmospheres. Yin et al. [ 13 ] processed pure yttrium (Y) decorated 316L powder under Ar–O 2  atmospheres with O 2  fraction of 1–2 wt%  and observed the formation of a Y 2 O 3  slag layer at the sample surface. Ikehata et al. [ 18 ] processed Fe–Ti alloys in pure N 2  atmosphere, causing the formation of a Ti(O,N) layer at the samples’ surface. The formation of slag layers in AM processes is also shown in simulations. It is predicted for low O contents originating from residual O from the process chamber or from the powder itself [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ]. However, the influence of slag layers on nanoparticle formation has not been studied in the literature to the best of our knowledge.

Several authors [ 13 ,  24 ,  25 – 26 ] observed large slag inclusions entrapped in their samples, similar to work of Felber et al. [ 27 ]. These micrometer-sized oxide particles originated from the slag layer and were caused by insufficient heat input ( E V ) during printing. Consequently, the question emerges as to whether nanoparticles also emanate from the slag layer. Moreover, it is relevant to investigate whether the slag layer can be used to augment nanoparticle formation. For that purpose, it is necessary to understand how slag layers form and how they can be manipulated. It is known that the slag layer thickness,  δ ox , increases with increasing energy input ( E V ) [ 27 ]. The volume fraction and size of the nanoparticles increase simultaneously.

In this work, the formation of slag layers and their influence on nanoparticle formation of pure Fe alloyed with 4.3 wt% Ti (designated as FeTi4.3) manufactured by PBF–LB in a reactive CO 2  atmosphere is studied. For this purpose, four different sets of experiments are conducted, investigating the effect of the powder layer thickness, build height, re-melting, and atmosphere on slag layer and nanoparticle formation. The manufacturing parameters,  P  and  v , were kept constant through all individual experiments as their effect on O uptake, oxide fraction and microstructure evolution was elucidated in [ 27 ]. The slag layer thickness and particle fraction are determined by optical and scanning electron microscopy and correlated with chemical analysis. The results obtained provide a fundamental basis for understanding the role of the slag layer in nanoparticle formation in additively manufactured ODS alloys.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Experiments were conducted with a powder blend consisting of Fe with 99.95% purity mixed with 4.3 wt% Ti Gd.1 using a Turbula (Willy A. Bachhofen) tumble mixing device. The tumble mixer operated at 70 rpm for four hours, ensuring a homogeneous powder blend. Fe powder was purchased by metals for printing (m4p) with a PSD of 15–45 µm, and Ti powder from Eckart TLS with a PSD of 20–63 µm. The composition of the elemental powders is given in Table  1 . CO 2  with a purity of 99.5% and Ar with a purity of 99.96%, supplied by Linde, were used for printing. Table 1 Chemical composition of Fe powder and Ti Grade 1 powder according to the certificate provided by the suppliers Element (wt%) Fe C O S P Fe Bal 0.003 0.09 0.0038  < 0.01 Element (wt%) Ti Fe O N C H Ti Grade 1 Bal 0.044 0.08 0.006 0.012 0.001

sections.heading: Manufacturing
paragraphs: An Aconity3D Midi + was used to print samples. It is equipped with an IR (λ = 1064 nm) fiber laser with a Gaussian beam profile, a spot diameter of 80 µm, and a maximum power of 1 kW. Samples were manufactured with  P  = 200 W and  v  = 800 mm s −1  to achieve minimum porosity. The powder layer thickness,  t , was set to 30 µm (“reference”), if not mentioned otherwise, and a 90° rotation strategy in between layers was chosen in each experiment. The hatch distance,  h , was chosen to be equal to the laser spot diameter using a bi-directional scanning strategy. The residual oxygen concentration in the process chamber was set to 0.04 wt% in each experiment. Residual O concentration is measuremend with a lambda probe. The gas flow was set automatically to approximately 13–16 l min −1 , which was necessary to keep an excess pressure of 50 mbar in the process chamber. Simple cuboids with varying sample geometry, depending on the experiment, were printed in CO 2  or Ar atmosphere. A summary of all samples for each print is shown in Table  2 . Table 2 Overview and description of samples of the four experimental series Designation t Atm Layer height Number of layers t = 15 15 µm CO 2 334 t = 30 30 µm 167 t = 60 60 µm 84 Build height Sample height 1 layer 30 µm CO 2 0.03 mm 5 layers 0.15 mm 10 layers 0.30 mm 30 layers 0.90 mm 50 layers 1.50 mm 100 layers 3.00 mm 200 layers 6.00 mm 400 layers 12.0 mm 600 layers 18.0 mm Re-melt Number of re-melting cycles 0× 30 µm CO 2 No re-melting 1× 1 × re-melting 2× 2 × re-melting 3× 3 × re-melting Multi atmosphere Sequence 100 CO 2 30 µm CO 2 3 mm sample printed in CO 2 100 CO 2  + R CO2 CO 2 Surface re-melted in CO 2 100 CO 2  + R Ar Ar Surface re-melted in Ar 100 CO 2  + 1Ar 30 µm Ar Printing 1 layer in Ar on top of CO 2 100 CO 2  + 10Ar 30 µm Ar Printing 10 layers in Ar on top of CO 2 100 CO 2  + 50Ar 30 µm Ar Printing 50 layers in Ar on top of CO 2 100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 1CO 2 30 µm CO 2 Printing 1 layer in CO 2  on top of Ar 100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 10CO 2 30 µm CO 2 Printing 10 layers in CO 2  on top of Ar 100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 50CO 2 30 µm CO 2 Printing 50 layers in CO 2  on top of Ar

The first experiment, “Powder layer height” (Fig.  1 a), consisted of three separate build jobs where the powder layer thickness,  t , was varied using 15 µm, 30 µm, and 60 µm. One cube (10 × 10 × 5 mm 3 ) for microstructure analysis and 10 cubes for chemical analysis (3 × 3 ×  5 mm 3 ) were printed in each build job. As the sample geometry is identical for all three build jobs, the number of layers required to manufacture the samples depends on  t,  which results in different total laser exposure times in the CO 2  atmosphere. The slag layer was removed mechanically for half of the samples for chemical analysis by grinding until all surfaces were bare metal, to reveal the O level in the bulk. Samples that were ground are designated as “w/o surface” and those that were not post-processed as “As build—AB”. Fig. 1 Experimental series 1–4:  a  Samples for microstructural analysis (10 × 10 × 5 mm 3 ) and chemical analysis (3 × 3 × 5 mm 3 ) to study the influence of powder layer height ( t  = 15 µm). The print jobs were repeated with  t  = 30 µm and  t  = 60 µm.  b  Samples consisting of different numbers of layers to study the influence of build height (1–600 printed layers). Samples for chemical analysis are extracted from the second cuboid, consisting of 600 layers.  c  Samples for microstructure and chemical analysis were manufactured with integrated re-melting. The number of re-melting cycles after consolidation of each layer varies from 0 to 3.  d  Samples were printed by alternating the process atmosphere. The base of each of the nine cuboids is the 100 CO 2  sample, which is the starting point for the eight other cuboids. + R displays samples that are once re-melted in Ar and CO 2 . + xAr displays samples with x (x = 1, 10, 50) layers printed in Ar on top of the 100 CO 2  sample. + xCO 2  displays samples with x (x = 1, 10, 50) layers printed in CO 2  on top of the 100 CO 2  + 50Ar sample. More details on each sample are given in Table  2

The second experiment, “Build Height” (Fig.  1 b), consisted of ten cubes with a dimension of 10 × 10 mm 2  and variable sample height (Table  2 ). The tenth sample was used for chemical analysis and is identical to the one with the largest height. For this purpose, the sample was cut into five blocks (10 × 10 × 3.6 mm 3 ) from which three samples each were cut for chemical analysis (4 × 3 × 3 mm 3 ). As all samples for chemical analysis were cut from one large cube, they are all in w/o surface state.

The third experiment, “Re-melt” (Fig.  1 c), covered four sets of samples. Each of the sets consisted of one cube (10 × 10 × 5 mm 3 ) for microstructure analysis and 8 for chemical analysis (4 in AB, 4 in w/o surface state, 3 × 3 × 5 mm 3 ). The sets differed in the number of re-melting cycles (0x, 1x, 2x, and 3x) applied to each layer. Re-melting was done directly after powder consolidation for each sample. For example, the one-time re-melting sample was exposed twice without interruption before the laser moved to the next sample.

The last experiment, “Multi-Atmosphere” (Fig.  1 d), consisted of nine identical cubes (10 × 10 × 3 mm 3 ) that were printed in CO 2 . After reaching a sample height of 3 mm (= 100 layers), the cubes were given 10 min to cool down. The first cube was the reference specimen (100 CO 2 ) and was not exposed to the laser anymore. The 2nd one was once re-melted without powder in CO 2 . Afterwards, the chamber was opened to remove the CO 2  from the build chamber and flooded with Ar for 90 min. Reaching an O level of 400 ppm in the chamber, the 3rd cube was once re-melted in Ar without powder. Before printing on top of the 4th-9th cubes was resumed, the platform was lowered by 30 µm, and the first powder layer was manually distributed on top of the samples. Printing was then continued under Ar atmosphere for the remaining six cubes. One layer was printed on top of the 4th cube (100 CO 2  + 1Ar), 10 layers on the 5th (100 CO 2  + 10Ar), and 50 layers on the 6–9th cube (100 CO 2  + 50Ar) before the job was paused again to switch to the CO 2  atmosphere, following the same procedure as switching from CO 2  to Ar. Subsequently, printing was continued in CO 2  on top of the three remaining cubes 7–9. This time, no re-melting was performed, and one layer was directly printed in CO 2  on top of the 7th cube (100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 1CO 2 ), 10 layers on top of the 8th cube (100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 10CO 2 ), and 50 layers on top of the 9th cube (100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 50CO 2 ).

sections.heading: Chemical and microstructure analysis
paragraphs: Samples were cut from the baseplates using a hand saw to avoid unnecessary heat input and contamination/corrosion by cooling liquids, both avoiding an increase in the O level during preparation. The oxygen content of the samples was determined using inert gas fusion analysis with an Inductar ONH (Elementar Analysesysteme GmbH). Three samples for each state were measured, and an average value was calculated.

The fraction of inclusions originating from the slag layer, designated as “slag particles”, was determined using one cross-section of a remaining sample for chemical analysis or, if not available, a corresponding sample from microstructure analysis. Images were taken with a Keyence VK-3000 confocal microscope, and slag particle content was determined with the software ImageJ.
This procedure was required as  δ ox  locally strongly fluctuates.

sections.heading: Reference state
paragraphs: Felber et al. [ 27 ] showed that processing FeTi4.3 (4.3 wt% Ti) in CO 2  leads to the formation of an approximately 5 µm thick slag layer (Fig.  2 a) on top and the sides of the samples as well as Ti-oxide nanoparticles (Fig.  2 b) with an average diameter of approximately 35 nm. The nanoparticle composition is assumed to be mainly TiO. Slag particles (Fig.  2 d) were incorporated in the bulk from the surface layer (Fig.  2 c), resulting from manufacturing with low heat input ( E V ). The oxygen in the samples is located in three forms: the slag layer, the slag particles, and nanoparticles. Fig. 2 Processing FeTi4.3 in CO 2  atmosphere causes the formation of  a  Ti-oxide slag layers on top of the samples and their sides and  b  Ti-oxide nanoparticles in the bulk.  c  The slag layer consists of two phases—Ti 2 O 3  (blueish-grey) and TiO (golden) as determined in XRD [ 27 ] from which d) micrometer size slag particles originate

sections.heading: Chemical analysis
paragraphs: The O content of the samples was measured in two states — AB and w/o surface. The difference between the two values is an approximation for the O content stored in the slag layer. Samples that are processed in CO 2  show a process gas uptake during manufacturing, compared to the powder level. Samples processed in Ar do not show process gas uptake and their oxygen level amounts to ca. 0.115 wt%, independently of manufacturing parameters or strategy. The overall O uptake does not appear to be significantly affected by the powder layer thickness used during printing (Fig.  3 a). A lower powder layer thickness increases the number of layers that are exposed during manufacturing for the same sample height. The O stored in the slag layer decreases with increasing  t , especially visible for the sample with  t  = 60 µm. Fig. 3 Chemical analysis of samples with  a  variable powder layer height,  b  along the build direction of the 18 mm high sample cut into 5 blocks, and  c  for samples using re-melting strategies. The composition is given for AB state (with the slag layer) and w/o surface state to measure the O stored in the bulk. The difference between the measurements corresponds to the O in the slag layer

The O concentration at different locations within the samples, measured in the five blocks along the build direction, is constant (Fig.  3 b). Note, no AB condition was measured for this experimental series, as the samples for chemical analysis were cut from the five blocks, which in turn were cut from a single cube with a dimension of 10 × 10 × 18 mm 3 .

The re-melted samples show a strong increase in the oxygen level in AB and w/o surface condition with an increasing number of re-melting cycles (Fig.  3 c). The increase in AB is larger than in the w/o surface condition, indicating that mostly the slag layer grows by re-melting. The increase in the w/o surface condition is either due to an increase in the nanoparticle fraction or the fraction of slag particles. Microscopy analysis is used in the following to break down the O distributions depending on the oxide forms and to explain the evolution of O concentration in the w/o surface condition.

sections.heading: Slag layer thickness
paragraphs: The slag layer thickness, δ ox , decreases with decreasing  t  and hence decreasing number of printed layers per sample (Fig.  4 a). However,  δ ox  strongly varies along the surface, which complicates interpretation. The deviations increase with increasing  δ ox . Fig. 4 Slag layer thickness  δ ox  at the top (brown) and at the sides (orange) of the cubes dependent on  a  the powder layer thickness used for printing,  b  the build height of the printed samples and  c  the number of re-melting cycles during processing.  d  shows the evolution of the slag layer when the atmosphere is switched from CO 2  to Ar and from Ar to CO 2  within one sample

The slag layer on top of the samples quickly grows with increasing number of printed layers from  δ ox  = 400 nm for the first layer, until reaching a maximum of  δ ox  ≈ 4.5 µm after ca. 50 layers (1.5 mm) (Fig.  4 b). This result shows that the slag layer accumulates upon printing until a certain constant thickness is reached.

δ ox  for re-melted samples (Fig.  4 c) is highly affected by re-melting cycles, as already determined from chemical analysis (Fig.  3 c). The slag layer at the sides strongly increases, whereas it decreases at the top of the samples. The decrease in  δ ox  at the top surface is counterintuitive, as it was expected that increasing the contact duration with the atmosphere would increase O uptake and hence  δ ox . The reason for this behavior is elucidated in the discussion part.

The reference sample for the Multi-Atmosphere experiments, consisting of 100 layers printed in CO 2  (100 CO 2 ), is covered with a 3.4 ± 0.3 µm thick slag layer on top. The build for this experiment consists of 9 of these samples, which serve as the basis for the Multi-Atmosphere experiments. Re-melting of the sample surface leads to an increase of  δ ox  to 4.1 ± 0.9 µm under CO 2  and 4.7 ± 1.0 µm under Ar (Table  3 ). Table 3 Slag layer thickness of 100 CO 2  + R samples in CO 2  (R CO2 ) and Ar (R Ar ), as well as for the reference sample (100 CO 2 ) from the multi-atmosphere experiments Slag layer thickness  δ ox 100 CO 2 3.4 ± 0.3 µm 100 CO 2  + R CO2 4.1 ± 0.9 µm 100 CO 2  + R Ar 4.7 ± 1.0

Printing is continued on the remaining samples in Ar, causing a drop in  δ ox,  which proceeds with printing further layers until the slag layer nearly disappears. The opposite behavior is observed when printing is continued under CO 2  on top Ar-processed samples (Fig.  4 d). The slag layer thickness increases similarly to that observed in the Build Height experiments (Fig.  4 b).

sections.heading: Nano particle analysis
paragraphs: The powder layer thickness (Fig.  5 a), build height (Fig.  5 b), and re-melting (Fig.  5 c) do not affect the particle size ( d p ), volume fraction ( f p ), and number density ( n p ) in the first two experiments. A slight trend towards larger particles and a lower number of particles might be visible for the re-melted samples with an increasing number of re-melting cycles (Fig.  5 c), probably due to heat up of the samples by the longer laser exposure time. Increased melt pool temperatures favor growth and accelerate Ostwald ripening of nanoparticles [ 28 ]. The sample manufactured with  t  = 60 µm (Fig.  5 a) and the one 3 × re-melted in each layer (Fig.  5 c) seem to be affected by process irregularities (e.g. recoating problems) as visible in Fig.  1 a and c, which could have influenced nanoparticle formation. Fig. 5 Ti-oxide nanoparticle mean diameter  d p , particle fraction  f p , particle number density  n p ,  and particle distribution dependent on  a  the powder layer thickness used for printing,  b  the build height of the printed samples, and  c  the number of re-melting cycles during processing.  d  shows the evolution of the particle size, fraction, and number density when the atmosphere is switched from CO 2  to Ar and from Ar to CO 2  within one sample. Note the different scale of ( a – c ) compared to ( d )

In contrast,  f p , and  n p  are highly affected by the process atmosphere used in the Multi-Atmosphere experiment (Fig.  5 d and Table  2 4 ).  d p  is slightly increased for samples printed in CO 2  compared to those printed in Ar. Particle analysis for these samples was done close to the sample surface to ensure probing in the upper-most layer, which is especially important for samples that consist of only one layer printed in the changed atmosphere or the re-melted ones. The reference sample of the Multi-Atmosphere experiments, consisting of 100 layers printed in CO (100 CO2), shows  f p  = 0.94 ± 0.18 vol%. Table 4 The mean particle diameter  d p , volume fraction  f p ,  and number density  n p  of 100 CO 2  + R samples in CO 2  (R CO2 ) and Ar (R Ar ), as well as for the reference sample (100 CO 2 ) from the Multi-Atmosphere experiments d p  (nm) f p  (vol%) n p  (1 × 10 19  m −3 ) 100 CO 2 22.1 ± 2.8 0.94 ± 0.18 1.10 ± 0.12 100 CO 2  + R CO2 21.9 ± 1.6 0.92 ± 0.16 0.99 ± 0.08 100 CO 2  + R Ar 21.8 ± 1.2 0.78 ± 0.13 0.83 ± 0.07

Re-melting in CO 2  (100 CO2 + R CO2 ) does not change  f p  significantly, whereas  f p  drops for re-melting in Ar (100 CO2 + R Ar ) (Table  4 ). The nanoparticle concentration further drops when printing is continued in Ar from  f p  = 0.62 ± 0.11 vol% for the first layer printed in Ar to  f p  = 0.40 ± 0.13 vol% after only ten more printed layers in Ar.

When switching back to CO 2 , the first printed layer in CO 2  contains a similar  f p  than under Ar, which is explained by dilution of the probed layer (100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 1CO 2 ) with the material printed in Ar below. This is the case as the melt pool depth is larger by a factor of 3–4 than the chosen layer height,  t , of 30 µm. After 10 layers printed in CO 2  on top of 100 CO2 + 50Ar, a comparable particle fraction and number density ( f p  = 1.04 ± 0.24 vol%,  n p  = 0.90 ± 0.03 × 10 19  m −3 ) are achieved as for the reference (100 CO 2 ) fully printed in CO 2 .

sections.heading: Slag particle analysis
paragraphs: The third form of oxide, besides in the slag layer and nanoparticles, which occurs in the materials, are slag particles. Slag particles are micrometer-sized oxide particles that are randomly distributed in the materials. As elucidated in [ 27 ], these slag particles originate from the slag layer, hence their name. Slag particles result when the energy input and thus the melt pool lifetime are insufficient. The slag layer breaks up upon laser exposure and causes large oxide particles to float in the melt pool. These large particles tend to float to the surface again to merge with the newly formed slag layer, driven by their lower density. Insufficient time to reach the surface (limited by the melt pool lifetime) causes their incorporation in the bulk [ 27 ].

The slag content amounts to 0.2–0.4 vol% in most samples not affected by manufacturing problems, which seems to be typical for the parameters used and is constant along the build direction (Fig.  6 a). Increasing the powder layer thickness,  t , reduces  E V  and results in porous samples that contain high slag contents (Fig.  6 b). Fig. 6 Sample overview at low magnification and their corresponding slag particle concentration (Vol%) measured for  a  the 5 blocks along the build direction corresponding to the area where samples for chemical analysis were extracted,  b  samples manufactured with different powder layer thicknesses, and  c  for samples exposed to re-melting.  d  shows a representative high magnification image of a highly porous area. The image is intentionally overexposed to make differentiation between slag and pore visible. Slag particles partially sit at the edges of pores

Re-melting strongly affects the slag particle content in the materials. One-time re-melting is favorable to reduce the slag particle fraction, whereas multiple re-melting (2x, 3x) increases the slag particle content again. However, it is not the re-melting itself that causes the slag but the associated overheating of the surfaces, which causes increased surface roughness and hinders the deposition of a clean powder layer that fully covers the samples.

Samples that are affected by recoating issues are often porous. The slag often sits at the edges of the pores (Fig.  6 d), which makes a proper analysis of the slag particle concentration by image analysis challenging and leads to overestimation of the real slag particle volume fraction. Avoiding these process irregularities comes hand in hand with limiting slag concentration in the samples.

sections.heading: Oxygen distribution
paragraphs: The data from microscopy, e.g. the slag layer thickness at the top and sides, the nanoparticle and slag particle fraction, can be used to calculate the corresponding fraction of O stored in the respective oxide forms (Fig.  7 ). This requires certain assumptions that are taken as follows: The slag layer composition used for calculation is Ti 2 O 3 . The limited amount of TiO contained in the layer is neglected for simplicity [ 27 ]. Slag particles are incorporated from the surface slag layer due to insufficient heat input during manufacturing. For this reason, the same composition, Ti 2 O 3 , as for the slag layer, is assumed. Nanoparticles have a composition of TiO according to the Fe-0.2O-Ti phase diagram (Fig.  7 ) and [ 18 ]. Fig. 7 Phase diagram of Fe0.2wt%O—Ti in the relevant temperature range for PBF–LB

The O content in TiO is 25 wt% compared to Ti 2 O 3  with 33 wt%. Calculation is done for samples with a dimension of 3 × 3 × 4 mm 3 , as used for chemical analysis. Details on the calculation are given in Appendix  1 .

Figure  8  summarizes the evolution of O in the slag layer (top and sides), slag particles, and nanoparticles, with the change of a certain parameter in one single graph. The O fraction resulting from chemical analysis (C) and based on microscopy analysis (M) is further compared. Determination of O levels in the materials based on image analysis (M) and chemical analysis (C) show good agreement in most cases. Only samples that contain a high content of slag particles show larger deviations between the two methods. The content of slag particles seems to be systematically overestimated. Fig. 8 Comparison of calculated O fraction divided into the slag layer at the surface, the slag layer at the sides, slag particles and nanoparticles based on microscopy analysis (M) and O fractions determined in chemical analysis (C):  a  variation of the powder layer thickness,  b  for different build heights and  c  for different number of re-melting cycles

Figure  8 a clearly shows that the powder layer thickness,  t , is not affecting oxide fractions unless the energy input,  E V , is high enough to result in a stable printing process. The nanoparticle fraction,  f p , and the slag particle concentration are constant along the build direction (Fig.  8 b). O levels determined by image analysis are slightly larger than those determined by chemical analysis, likely due to the overestimation of the slag concentration by image analysis. Re-melting causes an increased O uptake from the atmosphere, leading to enhanced oxide formation in the materials. However, mainly the O fraction of the slag layer and the slag particles is increased by re-melting, the O fraction of the nanoparticles is constant.

sections.heading: Correlation of slag layer and nanoparticle fraction
paragraphs: δ ox  and  f p  of the Multi-Atmosphere experiment are plotted together to determine whether the nanoparticle concentration and slag layer thickness are correlated (Fig.  9 ). Both curves show a similar evolution, but  δ ox  lags behind  f p  when starting to print in Ar and also when printing is continued in CO 2 . Fig. 9 Correlation of the average layer thickness at the surface with the particle fraction in the melt pool below. The red shaded area marks areas that are printed in CO 2  and the green ones in Ar

The reference state (100 CO 2 ) shows  f p  = 0.94 ± 0.18 vol% and  δ ox  = 3.4 ± 0.28 µm, which are both comparable with the values from the previous three experimental series. Similar values are achieved for the 100 CO 2  + 50Ar + 50CO 2  sample. After 50 layers printed in Ar on top of samples processed in CO 2  (100 CO 2  + 50Ar), the slag layer nearly vanishes, and the nanoparticle concentration is approximately halved ( f p  = 0.49 ± 0.09 vol% and  δ ox  = 0.28 ± 0.07 µm). After printing 50 layers in each of the two atmospheres, the values for  f p  and  δ ox  can be assumed to be representative of the respective atmosphere, Ar and CO 2 .  f p  is adapting faster to the respective atmosphere than  δ ox . 100 CO 2  + 10 Ar even shows a smaller  f p  than the one after + 50Ar, despite the sample being covered with a thick slag layer ( δ ox  = 2.29 ± 0.17 µm). The opposite holds for + 10 CO 2  on top of 100 CO 2  + 50 Ar, which is only covered with a thin slag layer ( δ ox  = 1.66 ± 0.64 µm). This is a strong indication that nanoparticle formation is not affected by an existing slag layer on top of the samples. + 1Ar and + 1CO 2  samples are affected by dilution with the material printed in the other atmosphere before. As mentioned before, this is the case as the melt pool depth is 3–4 times larger than the layer thickness,  t .

sections.heading: Manipulation of the slag layer thickness and its influence on nanoparticle concentration
paragraphs: Manufacturing in CO 2  causes a process gas uptake during manufacturing and hence increases the O level in the materials. CO 2  dissociates in two steps: CO 2  → CO + O and CO → C + O. Process gas dissociation is induced by laser exposure and occurs in the vicinity of the laser plume and causes an increased O partial pressure close to the liquid–gas interface [ 19 ]. The short laser exposure times and confinement close to the plasma plume complicate giving a value for the O partial pressure due to process gas dissociation. In-situ optical emission spectroscopy (OES) was currently applied in literature to investigate composition of the process atmosphere in AM [ 29 ,  30 ], and could be used in future work to define the chemical composition of the atmosphere in reactive atmospheres. Besides O partial pressure, chemical composition of the materials and temperature affects gas uptake in the materials. Further details are given in corresponding literature on high pressure casting [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ], which is believed to be applicable to our processes in AM. O concentrations reach values of up to 0.60 wt% in AB, and 0.15–0.25 wt% in w/o surface condition (Fig.  3 ). Measurements of the O level in the powder result in a concentration of ca. 0.105 wt%, which is slightly higher than specified in the supplier’s certificate. As a reference, FeTi4.3 samples processed in Ar have O levels around 0.115 wt%. The difference in O concentration compared to the feedstock powder is likely due to oxidation by the residual oxygen in the process chamber, which was kept below 0.04 wt% (400 ppm) in all experiments.

The O fraction determined by chemical and microscopy analysis shows, in general, good correlation (Fig.  8 ). But chemical analysis cannot differentiate between O stored in nanoparticles and slag particles, unlike microscopy analysis.

However, chemical analysis is more appropriate for obtaining a value for the slag particle concentration, due to their statistical occurrence, as explained in the following. Chemical analysis probes the full volume of the sample. In contrast, the determination of the slag particle content by microscopy is limited to a finite number of cross-sections. The quantification of slag particle content by chemical analysis, on the other hand, requires knowledge of the amount of O stored in nanoparticles. In this work, it was shown that, independently of the used strategy and for identical manufacturing parameters, the nanoparticle fraction in samples processed in CO 2  is constant. Thus, the amount of O stored in the nanoparticles remains constant and can be assumed to be roughly 0.15 wt% (c.f. 2 × re-melting samples with lowest slag particle fraction of 0.09 Vol%). The O excess above this value can be directly attributed to the O stored in slag particles (Figs.  3  and  6 ).

Variation of the powder layer thickness,  t , does not significantly influence the slag layer thickness,  δ ox , at the top and side, as long as  E V  is sufficiently high (Fig.  4 ).  E V  sinks with increasing  t , which causes the incorporation of slag particles from the slag layer when a certain  t  is overcome, which increases the O level in w/o surface state (Fig.  3 a). Thus, the incorporation of slag particles also reduces  δ ox  of the top surface (Fig.  8 a). Slag particle incorporation and process irregularities are strongly connected and can both be avoided when using optimum process parameters. The formation of slag in ODS materials manufactured by AM is only occasionally reported in literature, but often with an insufficient explanation for their origin [ 13 ,  23 ,  24 ,  25 – 26 ].

Re-melting is beneficial for decreasing the slag particle concentration in the materials (Fig.  6 ). Performing a single re-melting after each consolidated layer distinctly reduces the slag particle content. Re-melting most probably leads to a redistribution of slag particles from the bulk to the slag layer. The samples 100 CO 2  + R CO2  and 100 CO 2  + R Ar  from the Multi-Atmosphere experiments were only once re-melted and might also show an increase in  δ ox  compared to the reference, 100 CO 2 , for this reason (Table  3 ). However, overheating the samples by re-melting several times should be avoided, as this can lead to the opposite result, evident from the 2 × and 3 × re-melted samples. Overheating causes rough surfaces and even build-ups (c.f. Fig.  1 c) on which the powder cannot be deposited uniformly anymore [ 34 ,  35 ]. Re-melting increases the surface temperature of the samples with increasing number of cycles. This pre-heating effect causes a higher heat input and hence apparent value of  E V . Heat input by the chosen parameters for re-melting are not optimal anymore caused by the additional heat, which increases surface roughness and causes the recoating issues that lead to slag particle incorporation. The increased slag particle concentration in the 2 × and 3 × re-melted samples aligns with the decreasing  δ ox  at the top of the samples. Part of the oxide from the top slag layer is incorporated in the bulk as slag particles.

δ ox  at the sides is, in contrast, steadily increasing with increasing number of re-melting cycles. Slag at the sample’s side originates from the slag layer, which is dragged along the melt pool boundaries [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ,  27 ,  36 ] and is not re-melted during PBF–LB in case of the outer-most tracks. The driving force for material flow is mainly the marangoni effect, which is dependent on the surface tension and hence surface temperature distribution. Marangoni convections transports the slag towards the sides of the melt pool. Note, slag layers do not originate from solid state oxidation as they are too heterogeneous in thickness and their thickness is too high. Since the melt pool width typically exceeds the laser spot size, the laser would not directly expose the sides of the cubes during re-melting experiments. Consequently, slag at the sample’s sides accumulates with increasing number of re-melting cycles. Furthermore, repeated re-melting increases the surface temperatures and may promote evaporation of Ti-oxide due to its high volatility [ 37 ,  38 ]. This evaporation could explain the decreasing  δ ox  observed at the top surface, where the laser irradiates the surface. In contrast, the sample sides are not directly exposed to the laser and are not affected by evaporation for this reason.

sections.heading: The relationship of slag layer and nanoparticle formation
paragraphs: The increased O uptake from the atmosphere, e.g. by re-melting, promotes oxide formation in the materials. But the nanoparticle fraction,  f p , and number density,  n p , are in the same range for all samples processed in CO 2  (Fig.  5 ). Only samples that were re-melted show a slight increase in the particle size, which might be explained by the aforementioned pre-heating effect and higher apparent  E V . Instead, the increased oxide formation occurs via an increase in the slag layer thickness (Figs.  4  and  8 ).  f p  seems to be physically limited in the material for a certain set of manufacturing parameters, and excess oxide is always transferred to the slag layer.

The slag layer thickness accumulates with increasing number of layers until reaching a saturation value (constant thickness), when printing is performed in CO 2 , whereas an existing slag layer decreases upon printing in Ar, until it nearly vanishes (Figs.  4 b and  9 ). The formation and growth of slag layers is caused by O uptake from the CO 2  atmosphere, their reduction and disappearance by the absence of O uptake under Ar. The O uptake promotes nanoparticle formation. Thus,  f p  and  n p  are distinctly larger for samples processed in CO 2  compared to those processed in Ar.

Nanoparticle formation and slag layer formation are correlated, and both are enhanced due to O uptake during printing in CO 2 . However, the response of the slag layer is slow compared to nanoparticle formation when the process gas is changed (Fig.  9 ). An existing slag layer does not influence nanoparticle formation. In the performed experiments,  f p  and  n p  are solely dependent on the used atmosphere. Conversely, nanoparticle formation does influence slag layer formation, which is explained as follows:

The O solubility in Fe-Ti alloys is limited both in the solid and in the liquid state (Fig.  7 ), as Ti is a strong deoxidizer [ 39 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ]. This is the driving force for the formation of Ti-oxides in Fe-Ti alloys. During PBF processing, initially, Fe and Ti powder melt due to laser exposure and are mixed in the melt pool. Ti reacts with O from both powders and from the atmosphere. O uptake causes O supersaturation in the melt pool, which promotes (presumably liquid) nanoparticle formation, as absorbed O instantaneously reacts with Ti during manufacturing to decrease the O level in solution. This indicates that O supersaturation in the melt pool controls nanoparticle nucleation. Our model agrees with existing literature, describing nanoparticle formation and evolution during additive manufacturing processes [ 24 ,  28 ]. Nanoparticles grow in the melt pool and float towards the surface (negative sedimentation), once they reach a critical size, due to their lower density compared to the Fe–Ti melt (Stokes’ law) [ 43 ]. The still-liquid nanoparticles merge at the melt pool surface and form the slag layer. Nucleation and growth of nanoparticles, as well as negative sedimentation occurs within  t MP  (quasi steady state) and stop upon solidification. Rapid solidification freezes in the instantaneous microstructural state, including smaller nanoparticles levitating in the melt. Increasing  t MP  by re-melting strategies or decreasing layer height,  t,  merely prolongs the time available for these nanoparticle-removal processes but cannot increase  f p  and  n p  in the melt pool, as both quantities are limited by the negative sedimentation of the nanoparticles.

Kinetics of O uptake and oxide nanoparticles are fast considering melt pool temperatures distinctly above 2000 °C [ 44 ] and do not limit nanoparticle fraction. Previous work showed that oxygen uptake and slag layer thickness strongly and nanoparticle fraction slighly increase with  E V , explained by the increased time for gas uptake due to an increased melt pool lifetime [ 27 ]. Considering the low melt pool lifetimes of ca. 0.3 ms [ 27 ] in PBF, there is enough time for nanoparticles to float to the surface and form a slag layer with a thickness of 5 µm. Hence, kinetics are not limiting nanoparticle fraction but thermodynamics, e.g. O supersaturation in the melt pool dependend on the used atmosphere, does.

Although the evidence by the performed Multi-atmosphere experiments is indirect, the description of nanoparticle behavior in the melt pool is reasonable. More direct evidence would be possible using synchrotron experiments [ 45 ]. However, resolution in synchrotron experiments is often too low to resolve the ca 40 nm small nanoparticles and monitor their behavior in the melt pool. Furthermore, nanoparticle tracing by computanional fluid dynamics simulations could be used to predict nanoparticle behavior but requires an accurate model describing processes in the melt pool and experimental validation [ 46 ].

The laser breaks up the slag layer at the top of the samples when printing the subsequent layer, which results in micrometer-sized oxide particles (slag particles). The sedimentation velocity scales with the particle size according to Stokes’ law [ 43 ]. Therefore, slag particles (µm range) float faster to the surface to form the new slag layer than the nanoparticles (10 nm range), which reached the critical size [ 27 ]. Slag particle incorporation results when the time required to reach the surface is smaller than  t MP . Ti-oxide cannot dissolve during melting, considering the low O solubility in Fe–Ti, and hence accumulates at the top of the samples in each layer. This explains the growth of the slag layer from each printed layer until a constant thickness is reached. The nanoparticle fraction and slag layer thickness reached a constant value after approximately 50 layers as shown in the build height experiments. The nanoparticle fraction reaches a constant value already after 10 layers. Both values,  δ ox  and  f p  remained constant when printing up to 600 layers (20 mm). This result indicates that if parameters remain optimal during the printing,  δ ox  and  f p  remain constant when printing parts of bigger size.

The liquid slag layer on top of the melt pool might shield the melt pool from the atmosphere, prevent further gas uptake, and restrict its further growth [ 47 ]. The reduction of the slag layer upon printing in Ar might be explained by the incorporation of small slag particles (c.f. Fig.  6 a) in the bulk, which reduces  δ ox  after each printed layer. Measurement of the slag particle content showed that even under optimal parameters, slag particles (0.2–0.4 vol%) are observed in the materials. Promoted by higher O concentrations close to the liquid–gas interface and at the melt pool surface, further oxidation of the slag layer is likely [ 21 ,  22 ]. This might explain the occurrence of slag layers with a composition of mainly Ti 2 O 3  [ 27 ], whereas the nanoparticles are believed to have a composition of TiO, as predicted by the equilibrium phase diagram for FeTi4.3 (Fig.  7 ) and found in literature [ 18 ].

The nanoparticle fraction in additively manufactured Fe–Ti alloys is determined by processes forming nanoparticles, which are strongly dependent on the O supersaturation in the melt pool, and processes removing particles from the melt pool, via coarsening, floating up, and formation of the slag layer. While the latter processes are difficult to prevent, the former may be enhanced by increasing the activity of O at the atmosphere/melt pool surface. Thus, increasing the O partial pressure in the CO 2  atmosphere could be a potential strategy to increase particle formation, but it remains difficult to achieve, as most machines work under ambient pressures. Alternatively, more highly reactive atmospheres could be used to increase O uptake in the melt pool to increase particle formation. However, this strategy carries the risk of powder bed ignition or other safety risks [ 20 ].

For commercially available ODS steels, the oxide load is typically around 0.3–0.5 wt% and hence a little lower than achieved by the FeTi4.3 model alloys fabricated under CO 2  in this work [ 1 ]. The presented approach could therefore be an alternative to commonly applied ex-situ routes in AM of ODS materials. The work presented is furthermore relevant for ex-situ fabricated ODS alloys, as the melting point of the most commonly used oxides is overcome during AM [ 44 ]. Thus, nanoparticle coarsening as well as slag layer and slag particle formation by their floating to the surface are relevant for the fabrication of all types of ODS alloys in AM.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this work, the formation mechanism of the slag layer and in-situ nanoparticle formation, as well as their relationship, are studied for PBF–LB in a reactive CO 2  atmosphere. The following conclusions can be drawn: The formation of slag layers in PBF–LB is a cumulative process. The slag layer grows with an increasing number of printed layers until a constant thickness is reached, dependent on the used parameters. We argue that the slag layer forms from Ti-oxide droplets that are too large to levitate in the liquid melt pool, float up, and merge to form a liquid slag layer on top of the liquid melt pool. As manufacturing under CO 2  promotes particle formation (high  f p ), slag layers are growing under CO 2 , whereas existing slag layers are shrinking upon printing in Ar (low  f p ). Slag particles from the slag layer are incorporated into the materials when the heat input ( E V ) during manufacturing is not high enough or when process disruptions (e.g. recoating issues) occur upon manufacturing. The incorporation of slag particles reduces the slag layer thickness at the top of the samples. The nanoparticle fraction remaining in the melt pool is limited by nanoparticle flotation to the slag layer at the melt pool surface. Increasing the contact duration of the melt pool with the atmosphere thus only affects the thickness of the slag layer but does not assist in increasing the nanoparticle fraction. The nanoparticle fraction and number density are dependent on the process atmosphere only, for a certain set of parameters, and hence on the O supersaturation in the melt pool during processing, resulting from the respective atmosphere. Higher O supersaturation by O uptake during processing in CO 2 , enhances deoxidation reactions in the melt pool, causes more nanoparticle droplets to nucleate, and increases the nanoparticle fraction in the materials.
